methodology_note: Fairfax India is a closed-end/permanent-capital investment holding company (like Summerset's non-FCF treatment, but even more so - there is no operating FCF at all). Net earnings are pure mark-to-market swings on a ~70% Level-3 (illiquid, internally-modeled) Indian equity/infrastructure portfolio: FY2024 net earnings -$41.2M, FY2025 +$410.5M, Q1 2026 -$364.4M. A conventional FCF DCF is inapplicable - there is no distributable operating cash flow to discount. Instead this model projects Book Value Per Share (BVPS, the company's own primary performance metric and the basis for management's performance fee) forward 5 years, applies a scenario-specific EXIT PRICE-TO-BOOK multiple (calibrated to the stock's persistent post-2019 discount-to-book trading history), and discounts the resulting per-share exit value back at a cost-of-equity discount rate. No separate net-debt subtraction is needed because BVPS is already a per-share equity (post-debt) figure. No Gordon-growth terminal value is used; the exit P/B multiple IS the terminal value mechanism.

historical_growth.growth_divergence_warning: Revenue/EPS/FCF CAGRs are not meaningful for this entity - net earnings are mark-to-market portfolio swings (FY2024 -$41M, FY2025 +$411M, Q1 2026 -$364M), not operating income. BVPS CAGR (already net of the advisory + performance fee drag paid to Fairfax) is used as the sole growth anchor instead, per the book-value/holdco methodology. Note the Q1 2026 quarter alone saw BVPS fall 16.8% ($22.94 to $19.08) on Indian public-equity mark-downs plus rupee depreciation - the base-case 5-year projection starts from this depressed $19.08 base, which is itself conservative.

base.description: BVPS compounds ~8.5%/yr - between the 5yr (7.0%) and 10yr (9.2%) historical CAGR, reflecting India nominal GDP growth (~10-11%) less structural rupee depreciation (~2-3%/yr) less base+performance fee drag (~1.5%/yr), applied uniformly across 5 years (no deceleration needed since this is already a blended/normalized rate). Exit P/B of 0.80x reflects the persistent discount to book the stock has traded at every year since 2019 (versus 1.05-1.4x in the 2015-2018 period) - i.e., the market does NOT re-rate to book value even if BVPS keeps compounding.
base.terminal_growth_note: Not used as a Gordon-growth terminal value input (there is no perpetuity FCF); shown here for schema consistency and represents the assumed long-run nominal BVPS growth rate embedded in the exit multiple after Year 5 (India nominal GDP growth net of rupee depreciation, roughly consistent with the exit P/B being held flat rather than compressed further).

bull.description: BVPS compounds 12%/yr - the Anchorage/BIAL IPO (long-stop September 16, 2026) crystallizes value and shifts ~85% of the portfolio to public mark-to-market (from 31% today), Indian public-holdings marks recover from the Q1 2026 trough, and continued accretive buybacks below book add per-share value. Exit P/B narrows to 0.95x as the IPO catalyst plus improved earnings transparency closes most (not all) of the historical discount.
bull.terminal_growth_note: Long-run nominal BVPS growth context only; not a Gordon-growth input.

bear.description: BVPS compounds only ~4.5%/yr - rupee depreciation accelerates (as seen in Q1 2026's -5.2% single-quarter move), the Anchorage/BIAL IPO is shelved again past the September 2026 long-stop (as happened with the prior long-stop), Indian public holdings (IIFL Finance, CSB Bank, 5paisa, Fairchem) stay in a bear market, and further impairments occur (as with Sanmar sold well below carrying value in April 2026). Exit P/B falls to 0.65x, a 2020-style trough discount reflecting a loss of market confidence in Level-3 private marks.
bear.terminal_growth_note: Long-run nominal BVPS growth context only; not a Gordon-growth input.

base.note: BVPS projection only (no FCF); PV is computed once at the Year-5 exit value, not on interim BVPS marks, since there are no interim per-share cash distributions to discount.

wacc_rationale.components: Built up from: risk-free rate (~4.3% US 10yr, since USD-reporting) + equity risk premium (~5%) + small/mid-cap size premium (~1.5%) + emerging-market/India-specific premium (~1.5%) + governance/Level-3 valuation-opacity premium (~1%) + controlled-company (Fairfax 95.3% voting control vs 43.6% equity interest) discount-rate premium, netted against the diversification benefit of a multi-asset portfolio versus a single operating company. Bull case uses 10% (IPO catalyst reduces valuation-opacity premium); bear case uses 13% (elevated EM/currency/execution risk premium in a stress scenario). For reference, BIAL itself (the largest single holding) is internally DCF'd by the company at 12.2%-17.2% after-tax discount rates, consistent with the range used here at the holdco level.

sensitivity.sensitivity_axes: Axis 1 (rows) = cost of equity (WACC field, 9%-13%). Axis 2 (columns) = exit price-to-book multiple (stored in the terminal_growth_range field for dashboard schema compatibility, but values are exit P/B multiples 0.65x-0.95x, NOT a Gordon-growth terminal growth rate). Base-case Year-5 BVPS of $28.69 is held constant across the matrix; only the discount rate and exit multiple vary.

probability_weighted.rationale: Meaningful 25% bull weight is justified by the Anchorage/BIAL IPO long-stop date of September 16, 2026 being a real, near-dated, binary catalyst already on the calendar (not a speculative multi-year hope) that would mechanically shift ~54 percentage points of the portfolio from private Level-3 marks to public mark-to-market pricing.

sanity_check.diagnosis: Base-case IV of $13.62 implies 0.71x current BVPS ($19.08) and 0.59x FY2025 BVPS ($22.94) - both comfortably within, or below, the persistent 2019-2025 trading range of 0.6x-0.85x book, which is the expected result of discounting a 0.80x exit multiple back 5 years at 11% cost of equity. Bull case ($19.83) implies 1.04x current BVPS, at the high end of the historical range but still below the 2017-2018 peak of ~1.35x, consistent with a partial (not full) re-rating on the IPO catalyst. Bear case ($8.39) implies 0.44x current BVPS, below even the 2020 COVID trough of 0.60x, appropriately reflecting a severe stress scenario (IPO shelved again + accelerated rupee depreciation + Level-3 mark confidence crisis).

valuation_philosophy.summary: Fairfax India is a permanent-capital investment holding company, not an operating business - it has no product revenue, no operating margin, and no free cash flow to discount. Reported 'net earnings' are unrealized/realized mark-to-market swings on a ~70% privately-valued (Level 3, internal DCF) portfolio of Indian equity and infrastructure stakes, and have ranged from -$364M to +$411M across the last five reported periods alone. Attempting a conventional revenue-growth/FCF-margin DCF on this entity would either double-count value already embedded in Level-3 marks or produce a meaningless output driven by noise in quarterly realized/unrealized gains. Instead, the company's own primary performance metric - Book Value Per Share - is projected forward using a growth rate anchored to its 10-year (9.2%) and 5-year (7.0%) historical CAGRs, net of the base+performance fee drag already embedded in reported BVPS. A scenario-specific EXIT PRICE-TO-BOOK multiple, calibrated to the stock's own trading history (1.05-1.4x at IPO/peak, but a persistent 0.6-0.85x discount every year since 2019), converts the projected Year-5 BVPS into an expected per-share market value; that value is discounted back 5 years at a cost-of-equity rate built up from risk-free + equity risk premium + small-cap + EM + Level-3-opacity components. The exit P/B multiple functions as the terminal value mechanism - there is no separate Gordon-growth perpetuity calculation, because there is no perpetual free cash flow stream to grow.
valuation_philosophy.why_fcf_dcf_inapplicable: FCF DCF requires (1) operating cash generation distinct from investment marks, and (2) a stable margin/reinvestment structure to project forward. Fairfax India has neither: cash flow statement items are dominated by portfolio purchases/sales and mark-to-market non-cash items, and the 'business' is capital allocation into a concentrated, illiquid basket of Indian private and public holdings (BIAL alone ~55-62% of portfolio value) rather than a scalable operating model with a repeatable unit economics.
